entry.title: Google DeepMind Launches AlphaGenome Atlas
entry.content:
Techmeme | blog.google | hacker news

AlphaGenome Atlas is a 1-petabyte database that predicts the regulatory impact of every possible single nucleotide variant in the human genome. Using the AlphaGenome AI model, the platform maps 9 billion single-letter genetic changes across both coding and non-coding DNA regions to help clarify the functional significance of the genome.

The platform introduces the AlphaGenome Variant Impact (AVI) score, a single metric designed to help researchers quickly prioritize impactful variants for study. Researchers have already used the tool to identify a critical variant in the DNM1 gene for rare disease research and to uncover genetic regions linked to body mass index (BMI). The Atlas is accessible through a web portal requiring no coding skills.

Rentosertib, a TNIK inhibitor, has progressed to Phase III clinical trials to further evaluate its efficacy and impact on lung function.

entry.title: Fifth Circuit Affirms Dismissal of Jackson Water Contamination Lawsuit
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | motherjones.com | source | hacker news

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the dismissal of a lawsuit brought by Jackson, Mississippi residents alleging that the city's failure to prevent lead-contaminated water exposure violated their constitutional rights. Judge Kurt Engelhardt ruled that the U.S. Constitution does not grant a right to truthful information from officials or a right to clean water during a public health crisis.

The ruling follows years of infrastructure neglect in the majority-Black, high-poverty city, where lead levels have been a concern since at least 2015. While several U.S. states and various international governments have enshrined the right to clean water in their constitutions, the federal ruling limits the scope of such constitutional claims. The decision coincides with recent EPA proposals to weaken Clean Water Act protections.

entry.content:

A former 3M scientist, Kris Hansen, describes how the company knew for decades that perfluorooctyl sulfonate (PFOS)—a type of "forever chemical"—had spread into the blood of the general population and factory workers. Despite internal testing showing widespread contamination, the company maintained that the chemicals were not toxic and continued mass production of products like Scotchgard.

Hansen's findings revealed that the chemicals had entered the global food web, appearing in the blood of various animals, including birds and fish. This investigation highlights the widespread environmental impact of PFAS and the challenges of regulating chemicals when manufacturers withhold data regarding toxicity.

entry.title: UNEP Report: Global Temperatures to Exceed 1.5-Degree Warming Limit
entry.content:
Hacker News Best | pbs.org | source | hacker news

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report warns that Earth is expected to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius warming threshold established by the Paris Agreement within the next few years. The report outlines an "overshoot" strategy, suggesting that the world must first limit the peak temperature and then use carbon removal and fossil fuel phase-outs to return to safer levels to minimize long-term damage.

Current global policies project temperatures to reach 2.6°C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, though ambitious goals could cap warming at 1.8°C by mid-century. The transition period of overshoot is expected to last decades, causing increased extreme weather, rising sea levels, and food shortages. Experts emphasize that managing this period requires significant investment in climate adaptation and novel carbon dioxide removal technologies.
